run.name: Fdga 2026 Benchmark Congress
run.description: GerryChain ReCom MCMC ensemble — congress redistricting, 9,501 draws across 1 elections.

dem_seats.label: Seat–Vote Proportionality
dem_seats.headline: Does the seat count reflect how people actually voted?
dem_seats.description: In a fair map, the share of seats each party wins should reflect its share of statewide votes. This metric counts districts projected to lean Democratic based on each plan's vote patterns — not as a partisan goal, but as a measuring stick for proportionality. The histogram shows how many Democratic-leaning seats thousands of neutrally drawn alternative maps produce. If the enacted map falls far from this range, lines were likely drawn to systematically over- or under-represent one party.
dem_seats.takeaway: The enacted map produces 5 Democratic-leaning seats — at the 23th percentile, below the neutral median of 6 (range: 5–8). This is within the normal range for neutral maps, suggesting a structural seat advantage for Republicans.

formula_info.detail: dem_2pv_d = Σ dem_votes_vtd / Σ (dem_votes_vtd + rep_votes_vtd) for all VTDs in district d
formula_info.data_source: VTD composite — 2018–2024 five-election average (2018 Gov, 2020 Pres, 2021 Warnock runoff, 2022 Gov+Senate avg, 2024 Pres)

efficiency_gap.label: Wasted Votes Balance
efficiency_gap.headline: Are both parties' votes equally effective at winning representation?
efficiency_gap.description: Every election produces 'wasted' votes — votes cast in losing districts (all wasted) and surplus votes beyond what was needed to win (also wasted). A fair map wastes votes at roughly equal rates for both parties. The Efficiency Gap measures the difference: a positive value means one party's votes are being wasted at a higher rate than the other's — a sign that district lines are concentrating or dispersing that party's voters artificially. Developed by Stephanopoulos & McGhee; cited in federal gerrymandering litigation.
efficiency_gap.takeaway: The enacted map's efficiency gap (0.173) is above the neutral median (0.100), at the 96th percentile — outside the normal range for neutral maps. Democratic votes are wasted at a higher rate, giving Republicans a structural advantage in translating votes to seats.

formula_info.formula: (Σ wasted_dem − Σ wasted_rep) / Σ total_votes  across all districts
formula_info.detail: wasted_dem = excess Dem votes beyond 50%+1 in Dem wins + all Dem votes in Dem losses; symmetric for Rep

mean_median.label: Vote Distribution Symmetry
mean_median.headline: Does each party need the same number of votes to win a district?
mean_median.description: The Mean-Median difference reveals whether one party's votes are systematically spread more efficiently across districts than the other's. When one party wins many districts by modest margins while the other piles up large majorities in fewer districts, the map gives the first party a structural seat advantage — even when both parties receive equal votes statewide. A value near zero means both parties convert votes to seats at roughly the same rate. A large deviation in either direction is a signal of asymmetric voter distribution — often a hallmark of gerrymandering.
mean_median.takeaway: The mean–median difference (0.080) is above the neutral median (0.031), at the 100th percentile — an extreme outlier — this result would occur by chance in fewer than 1 in 40 neutral maps. Democratic voters are disproportionately concentrated in fewer districts, giving Republicans a more efficient geographic spread of support.

formula_info.detail: Positive → Dem votes distributed less efficiently across districts (Republican structural advantage). Negative → reverse.

comp_seats.label: Electoral Competitiveness
comp_seats.headline: How many districts give voters a meaningful choice?
comp_seats.description: A competitive district is one where the outcome is genuinely uncertain — where the margin between the two parties is within 5 percentage points of 50/50. Competitive districts force elected officials to be responsive to a broad range of constituents, not just their party base. Maps designed to protect incumbents — whether Republican or Democratic — tend to minimize competitiveness. This metric asks whether the enacted map produces fewer competitive districts than neutral alternatives would.
comp_seats.takeaway: The enacted map has zero competitive districts within the 5pp threshold. At the 6th percentile, this is toward the edge of the normal range. Every district has a predetermined partisan lean — voters have no meaningful choice in any race.

formula_info.detail: A district is competitive if the two-party Democratic share falls within ±competitive_margin of 50%

dem_safe_seats.label: Safe Democratic Seats
dem_safe_seats.headline: How many districts lean solidly Democratic — beyond the competitive margin?
dem_safe_seats.description: Counts districts where the Democratic two-party vote share exceeds 50% + 5pp — the outer boundary of the competitive zone. These seats are reliably Democratic and not meaningfully contested. Together with safe Republican seats and competitive seats, this completes the three-bucket political balance picture from the scorecard. An unusually high or low count signals packing or cracking of Democratic voters relative to what neutral geography-driven redistricting would produce.
dem_safe_seats.takeaway: Enacted value: 5.000. Neutral median: 5.000 (range: 4.000–6.000). At the 89th percentile — within the normal range for neutral maps.

formula_info.detail: Democratic-leaning districts outside the competitive zone — margin exceeds threshold on the Democratic side

rep_safe_seats.label: Safe Republican Seats
rep_safe_seats.headline: How many districts lean solidly Republican — beyond the competitive margin?
rep_safe_seats.description: Counts districts where the Republican two-party vote share exceeds 50% + 5pp — the outer boundary of the competitive zone. These seats are reliably Republican and not meaningfully contested. Together with safe Democratic seats and competitive seats, this completes the three-bucket political balance picture from the scorecard. An unusually high or low count signals packing or cracking of Republican voters relative to what neutral geography-driven redistricting would produce.
rep_safe_seats.takeaway: Enacted value: 7.000. Neutral median: 5.000 (range: 3.000–6.000). At the 100th percentile — an extreme outlier — this result would occur by chance in fewer than 1 in 40 neutral maps.

formula_info.detail: Republican-leaning districts outside the competitive zone — margin exceeds threshold on the Republican side

maj_black.label: Black Community Representation
maj_black.headline: Do Black voters have the opportunity to elect representatives of their choice?
maj_black.description: This counts districts where Black citizens make up more than 50% of the Citizen Voting Age Population (CVAP). Under Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, mapmakers must not draw lines that dilute minority communities' ability to elect their preferred candidates. The histogram shows how many majority-Black districts thousands of neutrally drawn alternative maps produce — establishing what geography alone would naturally support. The Princeton ensemble test treats deviation in either direction as a statistical anomaly: too few raises VRA dilution concerns; too many means the map is also unusual compared to neutral redistricting. Uses CVAP rather than VAP for precision (excludes non-citizens).
maj_black.takeaway: The enacted map has 4 majority-Black district(s) — more than most neutral alternatives (neutral range: 1–3). Black communities have strong electoral representation opportunity.

formula_info.detail: Uses Citizen Voting Age Population (CVAP, excludes non-citizens) for legal precision under Section 2 VRA. GerryChain: 2024 ACS 5-yr CVAP. ALARM: 2020 Census VAP.
formula_info.data_source: 2024 ACS 5-year CVAP disaggregated to 2020 blocks (GerryChain) / 2020 Census VAP (ALARM)

min_coal.label: Minority Coalition Representation
min_coal.headline: Do communities of color collectively hold electoral influence?
min_coal.description: This counts districts where voters of color — Black, Hispanic, Asian, and others — together make up more than 50% of the Citizen Voting Age Population. Even when no single racial group holds a majority, communities of color can collectively influence electoral outcomes. This 'coalition' measure is increasingly important as Georgia's demographics diversify. The Princeton ensemble test treats deviation in either direction as anomalous: the grade reflects statistical distance from neutral redistricting outcomes, not a policy judgment about the direction of that distance. Uses 2024 ACS 5-year CVAP estimates.
min_coal.takeaway: The enacted map has 5 minority-coalition district(s) — more than most neutral alternatives. Communities of color have strong collective electoral influence.

formula_info.detail: Combined non-white Citizen VAP share. A minority-coalition district is majority non-white but may include multiple racial groups, none individually a majority.

maj_white.label: Majority-White Districts
maj_white.headline: How many districts have a white-citizen majority of eligible voters?
maj_white.description: Counts districts where non-Hispanic white citizens make up more than 50% of the Citizen Voting Age Population. Shown alongside minority representation metrics to complete the full demographic picture of how the map distributes political power across racial groups. The Princeton ensemble test grades statistical distance from neutral redistricting outcomes symmetrically — unusually high or low counts compared to neutral maps both indicate the map departs from geography-driven redistricting.
maj_white.takeaway: The enacted map has 9 majority-white district(s), within the typical range for neutral maps (8–11).

formula_info.detail: Districts where non-Hispanic white citizens are a majority of eligible voters. Shown alongside minority metrics to complete the demographic picture.

min_influence.label: Minority Influence Districts
min_influence.headline: How many districts give communities of color meaningful electoral influence without a majority?
min_influence.description: Counts districts where communities of color collectively hold between the FDGA influence floor (37%) and the majority threshold (50%) of the Citizen Voting Age Population. These districts are below the threshold for direct Section 2 Voting Rights Act protection but above the level at which minority voters can meaningfully influence electoral outcomes and hold candidates accountable. More influence districts indicates broader minority electoral participation. Both thresholds are configurable.
min_influence.takeaway: The enacted map has 3 minority influence district(s) — fewer than 98% of neutral maps (typical range: 4–8). Communities of color have fewer districts where they can meaningfully influence electoral outcomes than neutral redistricting would typically produce.

formula_info.detail: Districts where communities of color have meaningful electoral influence but do not constitute a majority. Below the majority threshold for direct VRA Section 2 protection, but above the FDGA influence floor where minority voters can meaningfully affect outcomes.

muni_splits.label: Split Cities & Municipalities
muni_splits.headline: How many cities and towns are divided across different districts?
muni_splits.description: Counts incorporated municipalities (cities, towns) whose territory is split across two or more congressional districts. Urban cracking — dividing a city among multiple districts — dilutes its collective political voice and reduces the ability of city residents to elect a single representative who understands local concerns. Fewer splits means more communities are kept intact. The neutral ensemble shows how many splits geography-driven redistricting would typically produce; the enacted map is compared against this baseline.
muni_splits.takeaway: The enacted map splits just 12 cities and municipalities — fewer than 100% of neutral maps (typical range: 21–33). Urban communities are exceptionally well preserved compared to what neutral redistricting would produce.

formula_info.formula: count(municipalities m : ∃ VTDs v1, v2 ∈ m assigned to different districts)
formula_info.detail: An incorporated municipality (city, town) is 'split' when at least two of its VTDs are assigned to different districts. Urban cracking indicator.
